name: Jamnagar Refinery
capacity: 1.24M bbl/day — world's largest refinery
description: World's largest refinery complex. Processes Middle East and Russian crude for domestic consumption and export. Two adjacent refineries (DTA + SEZ) form a single mega-complex.

name: Ulsan Refinery
capacity: 840K bbl/day — Asia's 2nd largest single-site refinery
description: South Korea's largest refinery and a key node in Northeast Asian refined product supply. Major exporter of jet fuel, diesel, and petrochemicals across Asia-Pacific.

name: Ruwais Refinery
capacity: 922K bbl/day — expanding to 1.5M bbl/day by 2027
description: ADNOC's flagship downstream complex in Abu Dhabi's Western Region. Major expansion underway to become one of the world's largest integrated refining-petrochemical sites.

name: Ras Tanura Refinery
capacity: 550K bbl/day
description: Located at Saudi Arabia's largest oil export terminal. Integrated refining and export hub on the Persian Gulf coast. Critical node linking upstream production to global tanker routes.

name: Port Arthur Refinery
capacity: 626K bbl/day — largest refinery in the United States
description: Largest US refinery, wholly owned by Saudi Aramco through Motiva. Gives Saudi Arabia direct downstream presence in the US Gulf Coast refining corridor. Processes heavy sour crude.

name: Paraguana Refining Center
capacity: 955K bbl/day nameplate — largely offline due to sanctions and decay
description: Comprises Amuay and Cardon refineries on the Paraguana Peninsula. Once the world's largest refining complex, now operating at a fraction of capacity due to years of underinvestment, US sanctions, and operational failures.

name: Jurong Island Refining Complex
capacity: 1.5M bbl/day combined complex — Southeast Asia's refining hub
description: Jurong Island hosts multiple world-class refineries making Singapore Asia's refining and petrochemical hub. Strategic location on the Strait of Malacca controls fuel supply for all of maritime Southeast Asia.

name: Fos-sur-Mer Refinery
capacity: 210K bbl/day
description: Major Mediterranean refinery near Marseille. Key entry point for Middle Eastern and North African crude into Southern Europe. Part of the Fos-Lavera petrochemical corridor.

name: Rotterdam Pernis Refinery
capacity: 404K bbl/day — Europe's largest refinery
description: Europe's largest single-site refinery, located in the Port of Rotterdam — the continent's energy gateway. Supplies refined products to Northwestern Europe via pipeline and barge network.

name: Ras Laffan Petrochemical Complex
capacity: Condensate refining + petrochemical processing hub
description: Massive industrial complex adjacent to the Ras Laffan LNG terminal. Processes condensate from the North Field into refined products and petrochemicals. One of the world's most integrated energy-industrial zones.

name: Yanbu Refinery
capacity: 400K bbl/day
description: Joint venture between Saudi Aramco and China's Sinopec on the Red Sea coast. Processes Arabian Heavy crude. Represents China's direct stake in Saudi downstream operations and Red Sea energy logistics.

name: Shandong Independent Refineries
capacity: 4M+ bbl/day combined — China's largest refining cluster
description: Cluster of independent refineries in Shandong Province that collectively process more crude than most countries. Major buyers of sanctioned Russian and Iranian crude oil at discount. Largely outside state refiner control.

name: Jubail Industrial City Refineries
capacity: Multiple refineries totaling 800K+ bbl/day
description: World's largest industrial city. Houses SATORP (Aramco + Total) 400K bbl/day refinery and massive SABIC petrochemical plants. Central node in Saudi Vision 2030 downstream strategy.

name: Abadan Refinery
capacity: 400K bbl/day — historic, partially degraded
description: Once the world's largest refinery (built 1912 by Anglo-Persian Oil). Badly damaged in Iran-Iraq war, rebuilt but constrained by sanctions limiting spare parts and technology. Symbol of Iran's oil nationalism.
tag: HISTORIC — BIRTHPLACE OF MIDEAST OIL INDUSTRY

name: Dangote Refinery
owner: Dangote Group (Aliko Dangote — Africa's richest man)
capacity: 650K bbl/day — Africa's largest refinery
description: Opened 2024 near Lagos. Africa's largest oil refinery and the world's largest single-train facility. Aims to end Nigeria's absurd dependence on fuel imports despite being Africa's top oil producer.

name: Ras Laffan LNG Terminal
capacity: 77 MTPA — world's largest LNG export facility, expanding to 126 MTPA by 2027
description: World's largest LNG export terminal, fed by the North Field (world's largest gas reservoir). Qatar's North Field Expansion will cement its position as the dominant global LNG supplier through the 2030s.

name: Sabine Pass LNG Terminal
capacity: 30 MTPA — largest US LNG export terminal
description: America's first and largest LNG export terminal in Cameron Parish, Louisiana. Transformed the US from LNG importer to major exporter. Six operational trains. Key supplier to Europe post-2022 energy crisis.

name: Gorgon LNG
capacity: 15.6 MTPA — three trains
description: One of the world's largest LNG projects on Barrow Island, Western Australia. Supplies Asian markets, primarily Japan, South Korea, and China. $54 billion investment — one of the most expensive energy projects ever built.

name: North West Shelf LNG
capacity: 16.9 MTPA — five trains at Karratha
description: Australia's first LNG export project (1989). Located at Karratha in the Pilbara region. Pioneer of the Australian LNG industry that now supplies a significant share of Asia-Pacific gas demand.

name: Yamal LNG
owner: Novatek 50.1% + TotalEnergies 20% + CNPC 20% + Silk Road Fund 9.9%
capacity: 17.4 MTPA — Arctic LNG from Sabetta port
description: LNG plant above the Arctic Circle on the Yamal Peninsula. Pioneered Arctic shipping via Northern Sea Route to Asia. Joint Russian-Chinese-French venture. Symbol of Sino-Russian energy axis despite Western sanctions.

name: Bintulu LNG Complex
capacity: 29.3 MTPA — nine trains
description: One of the world's largest LNG complexes in Sarawak, Malaysian Borneo. Petronas flagship export facility supplying Japan, South Korea, and China. Malaysia is the world's 5th largest LNG exporter.

name: Tangguh LNG
capacity: 11.4 MTPA — three trains (Train 3 added 2023)
description: Located in Papua Barat, Indonesia. Third train expansion completed 2023. Supplies LNG to Japan, South Korea, China, and Indonesia's domestic market. Key to Indonesia's gas monetization strategy.

name: Ichthys LNG
capacity: 8.9 MTPA — two trains at Darwin
description: Japanese-led LNG project processing gas piped 890km from the Ichthys Field in the Browse Basin to Darwin. Japan's largest overseas energy investment. Ensures Japanese energy security from Australian gas.

name: Freeport LNG Terminal
capacity: 15 MTPA — three trains
description: Second-largest US LNG export terminal on Quintana Island, Texas. Suffered extended outage from June 2022 fire during peak European energy crisis. Key US Gulf Coast LNG export node.

name: Hammerfest LNG (Melkoya)
capacity: 4.3 MTPA — Europe's only large-scale LNG export plant
description: Europe's first and only large-scale LNG export facility, processing gas from the Snovhit field in the Barents Sea. Strategic importance surged post-2022 as Europe scrambled for non-Russian gas supply.

name: Bonny Island LNG (NLNG)
capacity: 22 MTPA — six trains, Train 7 under construction
description: Africa's largest LNG export facility on Bonny Island, Niger Delta. Chronic underperformance due to gas supply disruptions, pipeline vandalism, and Niger Delta instability. Train 7 expansion long delayed.

name: Golden Pass LNG Terminal
capacity: 18 MTPA — under construction, expected 2025-2026
description: Former LNG import terminal being converted to export facility at Sabine Pass, Texas. Qatar's major downstream investment in US LNG export capacity. Gives QatarEnergy direct access to Atlantic Basin markets.

name: Ghawar Oil Field
capacity: 3.8M bbl/day — world's largest conventional oil field
description: The world's largest oil field, producing since 1951. Single most important energy asset on Earth. Contains an estimated 170 billion barrels of reserves. Its decline rate is one of the most closely guarded secrets in energy.

name: South Pars / North Dome Gas Field
owner: NIOC (Iran) + QatarEnergy (Qatar) — shared field, separate development
capacity: World's largest natural gas field — 1,800 TCF reserves
description: The world's largest gas field, shared across the maritime border between Iran and Qatar. Qatar's side (North Dome) feeds Ras Laffan LNG. Iran's side (South Pars) is sanctions-constrained. The field that made Qatar the richest country per capita on Earth.
tag: WORLD'S LARGEST GAS FIELD — IRAN/QATAR SHARED

name: Permian Basin
owner: Multiple operators — ExxonMobil, Chevron, Pioneer, ConocoPhillips, Diamondback
capacity: 6.2M+ bbl/day (2025) — world's most productive oil basin
description: Spanning West Texas and New Mexico, the Permian Basin is the engine of the US shale revolution. Now produces more oil than every OPEC member except Saudi Arabia. Its output reshaped global energy politics.

name: Kashagan Oil Field
owner: NCOC consortium — Shell, TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil, KMG, CNPC, INPEX, Eni
capacity: 400K bbl/day (phase 1) — target 1M bbl/day
description: Massive Caspian Sea oil field, one of the largest discoveries in decades. Plagued by extreme technical challenges (high pressure, toxic H2S gas, freezing conditions). Cost over $50 billion — the world's most expensive energy project. Export dependent on CPC pipeline through Russia.

name: Prudhoe Bay Oil Field
capacity: 300K bbl/day (down from 2M peak in 1988)
description: Largest oil field in North America on Alaska's North Slope. Discovered 1968, peak production 1988. In terminal decline but still significant. Feeds the Trans-Alaska Pipeline to Valdez.

name: Tengiz Oil Field
capacity: 600K bbl/day (expanding to 850K with Future Growth Project)
description: Giant onshore oil field in western Kazakhstan discovered in 1979. Chevron's most valuable overseas asset. Future Growth Project (FGP) is one of the largest capital projects in the world. Export via CPC pipeline to Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk — a chokepoint vulnerability.

name: Burgan Oil Field
capacity: 1.7M bbl/day — world's second-largest oil field
description: The world's second-largest oil field after Ghawar. Discovered 1938, has produced over 65 billion barrels. Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait was partly motivated by control of Burgan. The field that funds Kuwait's sovereign wealth fund.

name: Safaniyah Oil Field
capacity: 1.5M bbl/day — world's largest offshore oil field
description: World's largest offshore oil field in the Persian Gulf. Produces Arabian Heavy crude. Part of Saudi Arabia's spare capacity buffer that gives OPEC its market-swinging power.

name: Cantarell Oil Field
capacity: 120K bbl/day (down from 2.1M peak in 2004)
description: Bay of Campeche super-giant field, once the world's second-largest producing field. Crashed from 2.1M bbl/day in 2004 to under 200K by 2014 after nitrogen injection failed. Poster child for state oil company mismanagement and depletion.

name: Pre-Salt Fields (Lula / Buzios)
capacity: 2.5M+ bbl/day combined from pre-salt layer (2025)
description: Deep-water pre-salt oil fields beneath 2km of ocean, 2km of rock, and 2km of salt layer off the coast of Rio de Janeiro. Made Brazil a top-10 global oil producer. Technically among the most challenging oil developments ever attempted.

name: Groningen Gas Field
owner: NAM (Shell 50% + ExxonMobil 50%, operated by Dutch state)
capacity: Being shut down — was Europe's largest gas field (peak 88 BCM/year)
description: Europe's largest gas field, discovered 1959. Production caused severe earthquakes in Groningen province, forcing a government decision to shut it down entirely by 2024. Closure during Europe's energy crisis forced greater dependence on Russian gas, then LNG imports.
tag: EUROPE'S LOST GAS GIANT — EARTHQUAKE SHUTDOWN

name: Leviathan + Tamar Gas Fields
capacity: 22 BCM/year combined — Israel's offshore Mediterranean gas
description: Offshore gas discoveries that transformed Israel from energy importer to regional gas exporter. Leviathan (2010) and Tamar (2009) supply Israel, Egypt, and Jordan. Potential linchpin of East Mediterranean energy diplomacy. Target of Hezbollah threats.

name: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
capacity: 6 GW — Europe's largest nuclear power plant (6 VVER-1000 reactors)
description: Europe's largest nuclear plant, seized by Russian forces in March 2022. All six reactors in cold shutdown since September 2022. Repeated shelling incidents raised global fears of nuclear disaster. IAEA maintains permanent monitoring presence.
tag: EUROPE'S LARGEST NUCLEAR PLANT — OCCUPIED WAR ZONE

name: Barakah Nuclear Power Plant
owner: Emirates Nuclear Energy Corp (ENEC) — built by KEPCO (South Korea)
capacity: 5.6 GW — four APR-1400 reactors, all operational by 2024
description: First nuclear power plant in the Arab world. Four South Korean-designed APR-1400 reactors. Supplies up to 25% of UAE electricity. Landmark of UAE diversification away from fossil fuels and strategic partnership with South Korea.

name: Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant
owner: AEOI (Atomic Energy Organization of Iran) — Russian-built
capacity: 1 GW — single VVER-1000 reactor (Unit 2 under construction)
description: Iran's only operational nuclear power plant. Originally begun by Siemens (Germany) under the Shah, abandoned after revolution, completed by Russia's Rosatom. Operational since 2011. Unit 2 under construction. Centerpiece of Iran nuclear debate.

name: Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant
capacity: 4.8 GW — four VVER-1200 reactors, first unit expected 2025-2026
description: Turkey's first nuclear power plant, fully owned and operated by Russia's Rosatom under an unprecedented Build-Own-Operate model. Russia will own the plant on NATO soil for its operational lifetime. Strategic Russian leverage over a NATO member.
tag: RUSSIAN NUCLEAR PLANT ON NATO SOIL

name: Hinkley Point C Nuclear Power Station
capacity: 3.2 GW — two EPR reactors, under construction
description: UK's first new nuclear plant in a generation. Massive cost overruns (now over 35 billion GBP) and repeated delays. Chinese state-owned CGN holds a 33.5% stake, raising security concerns. Symbol of both nuclear ambition and construction dysfunction.
tag: UK NUCLEAR — OVER BUDGET, CHINESE STAKE

name: Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant
capacity: 2 GW operational (Units 1-2), expanding to 6 GW (6 reactors planned)
description: India's largest nuclear power plant at the southern tip of Tamil Nadu. Russian-built VVER-1000 reactors. Expansion from 2 to 6 reactors underway. Cornerstone of Russia-India nuclear energy cooperation and India's energy security strategy.

name: Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant
owner: Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission — Russian-built Rosatom
capacity: 2.4 GW — two VVER-1200 reactors, under construction
description: Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant on the Ganges river. Russian-built with $12.65 billion Russian financing. Extends Rosatom's influence into South Asia. Unit 1 expected to commission 2025.

name: El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant
capacity: 4.8 GW — four VVER-1200 reactors, under construction
description: Egypt's first nuclear power plant on the Mediterranean coast. Russian-built with $25 billion Russian loan covering 85% of cost. Gives Rosatom a Mediterranean footprint and extends Russian energy influence into North Africa.

name: Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant
owner: Armenian Nuclear Power Plant CJSC (state) — Soviet-era design
capacity: 448 MW — single VVER-440 reactor (Unit 2), Unit 1 decommissioned
description: Soviet-era nuclear plant providing ~30% of Armenia's electricity. Located in a seismic zone 30km from Yerevan. No containment dome. EU and Turkey have urged closure for decades. Armenia has no alternative baseload power, making shutdown politically impossible.

name: Olkiluoto 3 Nuclear Reactor
owner: TVO (Teollisuuden Voima) — EPR reactor built by Areva/Siemens
capacity: 1.6 GW — Europe's largest nuclear reactor
description: Europe's largest nuclear reactor, finally operational in April 2023 after 18 years of construction delays and massive cost overruns (original 3 billion EUR became 11+ billion). Now provides ~15% of Finland's electricity. Its troubled construction nearly killed the EPR reactor design.
